title: Enums, Tuples & Const Assertions
description: String/numeric/const enums, when to prefer union literals, tuples, and const assertions for immutable inference.

challenges.title: String enum vs union literal
challenges.whyMatters: Most TypeScript style guides (including Google and Airbnb) now prefer union literals over enums. Knowing why helps you read legacy code and make informed choices in new projects.
hints: Enums compile to JavaScript objects; union literals are erased at compile time

choices.label: Enums exist at runtime as JavaScript objects and add bundle size; union literals are compile-time only and produce no output
Union literals are faster at runtime
Enums support more values than union literals

challenges.title: const enum — inlined values
challenges.whyMatters: const enums are inlined at compile time — no runtime object, no bundle cost. But they break in certain module configs (isolatedModules). Knowing this prevents mysterious build failures.
hints: const enum values are substituted inline by the compiler — no JavaScript object is emitted

choices.label: const enum is the same as enum but declared as a constant
const enum values are inlined at compile time — no runtime object is created, but they break under isolatedModules
const enum is deprecated and should not be used
const enum creates a frozen object at runtime

challenges.title: Tuple types
challenges.whyMatters: Tuples let you return multiple typed values from a function without a named object — common in Go-style error returns and React-style hooks.
hints: A tuple is an array with fixed positions and fixed types at each position

choices.label: result is (number | boolean)[] — TypeScript doesn't know which is which
result is [number, boolean] — value is number, ok is boolean, positions are known
result is any[] — tuples are not typed
result is { 0: number, 1: boolean } — tuples compile to objects

challenges.title: Write functions using tuples
challenges.description:
Write these tuple-returning functions:

1. `trySplit(input: string, delimiter: string): [string[], boolean]`
   — splits the string; if delimiter not found returns `[[input], false]`; otherwise `[parts, true]`

2. `minMax(nums: number[]): [number, number]`
   — returns `[min, max]`; throws Error `'Empty array'` if empty

3. `parseKeyValue(line: string): [string, string] | null`
   — parses `'KEY=VALUE'` format; returns `[key, value]` or null if format is wrong
challenges.whyMatters: These patterns appear in config file parsers, log line processors, and CLI output parsers — all common scripting tasks.
hints: JavaScript has built-in functions that find the minimum and maximum of a set of numbers — spread the array to pass all elements as individual arguments
parseKeyValue: use indexOf('=') — if -1 return null, else slice at the index

challenges.title: const assertion — as const
challenges.whyMatters: `as const` is used to freeze config objects so their values become literal types — essential when you want TypeScript to know the exact value, not just the type.
hints: as const narrows every value to its literal type and makes the object deeply readonly

choices.label: No difference — as const is just a style hint
config2 has type { readonly host: 'localhost'; readonly port: 8080 } — literal types, not string/number
config2 is frozen at runtime via Object.freeze

challenges.title: Use as const for typed config
challenges.description:
Define a config using `as const`:

```
const ENVIRONMENTS = ['prod', 'staging', 'dev'] as const
const LOG_LEVELS = ['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error'] as const
```

Derive these types from the const arrays (no manual type literals):
- `Environment` — union of ENVIRONMENTS values
- `LogLevel` — union of LOG_LEVELS values

Write:
- `isEnvironment(val: unknown): val is Environment` — type guard using the array
- `isLogLevel(val: unknown): val is LogLevel` — type guard using the array
- `parseEnv(val: unknown): Environment` — uses isEnvironment, throws if invalid
- `parseLogLevel(val: unknown): LogLevel` — uses isLogLevel, throws if invalid
challenges.whyMatters: Deriving union types from const arrays means adding 'canary' to ENVIRONMENTS automatically updates the union everywhere — single source of truth for valid values.
hints: To derive the union type from the const array, use typeof on the array and index it with number — this extracts each element literal type as a union
Cast the const array to a readonly string array for the includes check — then cast val to string so TypeScript accepts it as the argument
Call the type guard — if it passes, return the validated value (TypeScript narrows it automatically); otherwise throw an error describing the invalid input

challenges.title: Labeled tuples and rest elements
challenges.description:
Write these advanced tuple patterns:

1. A function `httpResponse` with labeled tuple return type:
   `[status: number, body: string, headers: Record<string, string>]`
   — returns a 200 response with given body and empty headers by default

2. A function `spread` that accepts a rest tuple:
   `function spread<T extends unknown[]>(first: string, ...rest: T): [string, ...T]`
   — prepends first to rest

3. A function `zipPairs` that takes two arrays and returns an array of `[string, number]` tuples:
   `zipPairs(keys: string[], values: number[]): [string, number][]`
   — pairs by index, stops at the shorter array
challenges.whyMatters: Labeled tuples appear in typed middleware chains and request/response pipelines. Rest tuples are used in typed decorator and higher-order function patterns.
hints: Labeled tuple: type Response = [status: number, body: string, headers: Record<string, string>]
Prepend first to the rest elements in the return array — cast it to the labeled tuple type to satisfy TypeScript
zipPairs: use Math.min(keys.length, values.length) for the loop bound
